newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina lobbies Shalikashvili for U.S. ally status.
newsitem.headline: Argentina lobbies Shalikashvili for U.S. ally status.

text.p: Argentina urged the U.S. military's top officer Gen. John Shalikashvili on Thursday to grant it "major non-Nato ally status" in recognition for its military support and to help it buy new military hardware.

The chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff told a news conference in Buenos Aires with his Argentine counterpart Adm. Jorge Enrico that Washington was "very carefully reviewing" Argentina's request to be granted special ally status.

President Carlos Menem is eager for recognition for making Argentina one of the strongest U.S. allies in South America, for its military support role in the Gulf War and its role in international peacekeeping from Croatia to Cyprus and Haiti.
But Argentina -- which has slashed defence spending and ended conscription since its return to democracy in 1983 -- does not just want recognition.
Enrico said special ally status "might have further consequences, very important from the military point of view, if it means making it easier for Argentina to acquire war materiel it needs."

The general, who met Menem during a two-day visit, pinned the Joint Meritorious Unit Award medal on the chests of Argentine soldiers who worked with U.S. forces keeping peace on the border between Peru and Ecuador. Argentine, Chilean and Brazilian troops are the first foreigners to get the medal.

Shalikashvili praised the new climate of peace and military cooperation in southern South America, with Argentina and Chile putting aside their history of border rows to plan joint military exercises, as a "dream coming true."

"Probably out of all the regions in the world that you can think of now, this region is truly a success story in that the threats that existed before whether they were coming from border disputes and what not are all being resolved," he said.
But the general, who steps down in September, said the prospect of special ally status for Argentina would not herald a new U.S. military relationship with the whole region.

"That kind of major non-Nato ally status is conferred on very few countries and only those countries with which the United State feels it is import to signal a special relationship," the U.S. Army general said. "It ought not be viewed as some sort of first cornerstone of a wider military alliance in this region."

Washington has still not lifted its virtual ban on the sale of high-tech arms to Latin America, imposed when much of the region was under military dictators, and kept in place because of fears that sophisticated weapons sales could unleash an arms race in Latin America.

President Bill Clinton has been urged by aides to end the ban, which could open a lucrative market to the U.S. defence industry for now democratic Latin American nations eager to update their out-of-date military hardware.
But Shalikashvili told Reuters the policy was still "under review in Washington to see if in fact changes ought to be made to take into account the new realities that exist."
Clinton is scheduled to visit Argentina and Brazil in October and U.S. officials say a decision could be made by then.
